# Google Deepmind's "Humanity's First Exam" shows top AI models still fail simple everyday tasks under repeated runs

Nano Banana prompted by THE DECODER

**Google Deepmind wants to measure AI reliability rather than peak performance with "Humanity's First Exam."Early results show top models can solve nearly every task family at least once. Still, no model stays error-free across all repeated runs and variations.**

The benchmark's name plays off the well-known "Humanity's Last Exam" AI test, which takes the opposite approach by using highly complex tasks to test peak performance.

content_en:
# Robotics startup Embo raises $110 million in seed funding to build world-model AI for robots

**Robotics AI startup Embo has raised $110 million in seed funding to build AI models for smarter everyday robots.** Andreessen Horowitz led the round, joined by Khosla Ventures, DST Global, and Nvidia, Embo says. Its unified model pretrains on large amounts of internet video as a world model that learns how objects and physical interactions work. The AI then practices motor skills in simulated scenarios before fine-tuning on experience from a humanoid robot fleet.

The team says it worked on Dreamer, VideoGPT, and Diffusion Forcing and brings experience from Google Deepmind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, Nvidia Cosmos, UC Berkeley, and MIT. Today's robots often fail in unfamiliar situations. Embo says it's countering that by training a model from scratch with reinforcement learning.

Embo isn't alone. In robotics, world action models are seen as the next paradigm, where world models feed imagined future frames into a pretrained robotics AI. Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li founded World Labs in 2024 and raised $230 million for spatial intelligence, also backed by Andreessen Horowitz and Nvidia. Our Frontier Radar #5 deep dive covers the new AI labs and their bets, including World Labs, which will soon operate under AMD.

# Terence Tao sees AI ushering in "Big Math," but calls major tech firms' proofs "toxic waste"

**Renowned mathematician Terence Tao expects AI to overhaul how his field is organized.** On the Hard Fork podcast, he calls this "Big Math," paralleling the decades-old "Big Science" model. Mathematicians will collaborate in ever larger groups, he says, with even postdocs and PhD students leading ambitious projects because AI speeds up entry into complex topics. Human-AI teams could systematically map thousands of problems rather than solving them individually. Tao described a similar "industrialization of mathematics" in 2024.

Still, he sharply criticizes current AI results from major tech companies. The models solve open problems and contribute technically, he says, but produce answers without understanding and can't explain their proofs. Such proofs are "toxic waste" to those companies, in his view: an unwanted byproduct of training better models that firms must dump after minimal cleanup. In October, Tao and other mathematicians called for an OpenAI boycott.

He's equally critical of AI-generated papers flooding academic journals. They sometimes solve open problems, he says, but often fail to open new research directions, cite sloppily, explain poorly, and aren't enjoyable to read. Eventually, Tao hopes AI will deliver the "first awful solution," and humans will structure it properly and put it into clear context.

title: AI data center boom strains construction labor across the U.S.
excerpt: CNBC traveled to Abilene, Texas to see how the AI data center construction boom is impacting the local economy in both positive and negative ways.
title_en: AI data center boom strains construction labor across the U.S.
excerpt_en: CNBC traveled to Abilene, Texas to see how the AI data center construction boom is impacting the local economy in both positive and negative ways.
content_en:
President Donald Trump said last week that American companies will face a "tremendous tax" for building data centers outside of the U.S.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything," Trump said at the end of that week's major tech stock selloff.

Amid the nationwide public backlash against data centers and the ongoing market turmoil affecting the artificial intelligence industry itself, there's a more pressing problem with Trump's demand — a worker shortage.

Across the country, tech companies are already competing for a limited pool of electricians, plumbers and other skilled construction workers needed to erect the massive facilities powering the AI boom. Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) estimates the construction industry needs to attract 349,000 net new workers in 2026 just to keep pace with demand.

The pressure is hitting home in Abilene, Texas, where thousands of workers have descended on the region to build massive data center projects. RV parks and temporary housing have expanded to accommodate the influx, while local homebuilders and contractors say they're losing skilled workers to data center jobs offering substantially higher pay.

For Abilene homebuilder Gene Lantrip, the boom has become what he calls "a two-edged sword." Data centers are bringing new business and residents to the city, while making it harder and more expensive to find the workers.

Skilled laborers have been flocking to Texas in droves since 2025 to construct massive data center facilities like the $500 billion Stargate Project for OpenAI, Oracle and Japan's SoftBank. The vast prairie surrounding Abilene is now adorned with mile-wide construction sites and a collection of RV parks and mobile homes to accommodate the region's new blue-collar residents.

Tech giants have pitched these gigantic data center facilities as necessary to train and run powerful foundation models. And because these tech firms want data center campuses to come online quickly, they've been luring construction workers around the U.S. with lavish pay packages to settle down in rural places like Richland Parish, Louisiana, which will be home to Meta's over $50 billion Hyperion data center.

Lantrip said "the economy of Abilene is great because of the data center" and he's busier than ever building houses to accommodate the multitude of new residents. But the overall cost and time to build homes is increasing due in part to having a smaller pool of workers to hire from, he said.

Scotty Wristen, an Abilene master electrician who works with Lantrip, said that some of his electricians decamped to work on AI data centers because of the better pay. Even the local commercial electrical companies in the area have lost workers to the AI data centers, he said.

"I know of one company that lost 42 guys in one day," Wristen said. "If I was young and didn't have a wife and kids, I would probably do it too, because they pay at least triple what I can pay."

Those jobs also include on-the-job training, sponsored by the tech companies.

To boost the supply of construction workers, tech giants like Meta, Google and Amazon are spending millions of dollars on training programs that place aspiring builders at data center sites for hands-on, paid experience. The ABC is currently partnering with Meta on the social media giant's $115 million American Workforce Academy, pitched as "a nationwide, unprecedented fast-track to a long-term career in a skilled trade."


Meta's training program has so far "attracted thousands of folks who want to get into construction and learn a trade and to eventually work in data centers," said Joel Thames, an ABC vice president of health safety, environment and workforce development.

It's unclear what happens to towns like Abilene and the throng of data center construction workers once they finish building the facilities. Tech companies will have a tougher time initiating new data center buildouts in the U.S. following the midterm elections in which voters overwhelmingly supported various restrictions on data center related projects.

Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for a statewide data center moratorium until additional rules are in place giving residents more agency to determine whether new facilities should be built. For data center real estate developers like Anita Verma-Lallian, who has projects in Texas and Arizona, any restrictions placed on new initiatives may speed up the completion of the existing buildout.

"What's happened in my view, it's just going to make the demand even higher because the supply is going to be so much more constrained," Verma-Lallian, the CEO of Arizona Land Consulting, said. "We're going to see a rush to get those projects built and online as soon as possible."

Verma-Lallian said that there is "going to be some uncertainty" for potential new data center projects in Texas due to any yet-to-be-known restrictions. She views Arizona as being a more favorable environment to data center development and noted that Democratic incumbent Governor Katie Hobbs is "fairly moderate on data centers." 

If data center construction eventually slows in places like Texas, Verma-Lallian said it's possible that the new labor diaspora "will go to other states or other projects."

**WATCH**: **CNBC traveled to Abilene, Texas to see how the AI data center construction boom is impacting the local economy.** 

*CNBC's Jeniece Pettitt and Cameron Costa contributed to this report.*

title: Sakana AI’s CEO says its homegrown models are about more than Japan’s national security
excerpt: Sakana AI aims to strengthen Japan’s industrial competitiveness with homegrown AI models.
title_en: Sakana AI’s CEO says its homegrown models are about more than Japan’s national security
excerpt_en: Sakana AI aims to strengthen Japan’s industrial competitiveness with homegrown AI models.
content_en:
Sakana AI, a Japanese AI startup, last month revealed plans to develop its own foundation model. The move has drawn attention for its potential impact on Japan’s defense and cybersecurity sectors as well as concerns about reliance on U.S. and Chinese technologies.

Sakana AI’s co-founder and CEO, David Ha, told TechCrunch that its upcoming foundation model, Sawara, is part of the company’s broader goal of supporting and strengthening Japan’s industrial and manufacturing sectors using AI. In addition, Ha noted rising cybersecurity threats and stressed the need for domestic AI alternatives for sensitive applications, particularly if access to foreign models becomes limited.

“When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do. This is our long-term vision,” Ha said. “But short-term, I think Japan has a real need for security-related capabilities as well.”

Sakana will begin working on Sawara this month, aiming to train and release a smaller-scale model in early 2027, followed by a larger version.

The project comes roughly five months after Sakana launched Fugu, an AI orchestration system that ropes in other large language models, including those developed by U.S. AI labs, to assemble AI agents according to the task at hand. The Tokyo-based startup has also built Namazu, a Japanese-focused language model that fine-tunes existing open-weight models from Meta and DeepSeek to better understand Japanese language, culture, and business needs, including translation, political questions, and AI agent tasks.

“We cannot simply use open-weight models as-is in Japan for enterprises because they’re usually biased towards their creators,” Ha said. “They may refuse to answer questions about Japan or Japanese politics \[…\] they may give Japanese people answers they don’t want to hear.”

However, Ha acknowledged that developing a domestic foundation model alone will not fully eliminate reliance on foreign AI technology.

“The only thing \[left\] for us to become a full-stack company is the pre-training, Sawara,” Ha continued. “We plan to apply the \[Sawara\] technology in industry and manufacturing. We’ll train both a small and a large model next year. The small model should be particularly useful for on-premises solutions. Japan needs on-premises deployment capabilities.”

While Fugu incorporates OpenAI’s models, Ha noted that foreign AI models are not enough for certain applications. For example, in cybersecurity, Japan requires that customized models be deployed on-premises.

“Japan will continue to use U.S. systems, but it also wants domestic alternatives,” Ha said. “People often point to Palantir and other systems. I have a great deal of respect for companies such as Snowflake, Palantir, and Datadog. But for national defense, Japan will want its own systems.”

Sakana signed a research contract with Japan’s Ministry of Defense in July to explore how AI could help analyze and integrate information from multiple sources, and it has also worked with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, on systems for detecting disinformation.

Sakana’s work with Japanese government agencies has shaped its approach to developing Sawara, Ha said. Unlike commercial customers, government agencies often have stricter requirements, including the ability to audit training data, customize AI models and deploy them on-premises.

“Those lessons helped us plan how to develop and deploy Sawara. I think similar requirements exist in many governments,” he said.

While enterprise customers can use a combination of Fugu, Namazu and AI models developed overseas, Sakana’s government-related work currently focuses on two main areas: disinformation detection and analysis, and multimodal systems that integrate data from different government sources.

## Going public in Japan

Sakana’s expansion into developing its own foundation models comes amid speculation about a potential IPO following reports by Nikkei and Bloomberg earlier this month.

But Ha said the company doesn’t have any near-term plans to go public.

The reported timing and potential valuation were speculative, Ha said, adding that he did not know when the company might pursue a listing, though he expects his startup to eventually go public in Japan itself.

“We have a gravitational pull to eventually IPO in Japan,” Ha said.

Ha sees Sakana’s future growth tied to the global expansion of Japanese manufacturers. Rather than focusing on selling its models, the company wants to help local companies use AI to become more competitive globally.

“We want to strategically work with the government and Japanese industrial base, make them competitive,” Ha said. “We want to go abroad, go international together with manufacturing and industrial sectors.”
